Prompting a Builder from a Spec

How precisely must a product manager write for a builder — human or AI — to build what she actually meant, and what happens in the twenty-one hours between an ambiguous sentence and a precise one?

A Tuesday morning in Bengaluru

On the morning of 9 March 2026, Kavya Menon, senior product manager at Panchali Commerce Cloud, opened a pull request she had not asked for and did not recognise. Panchali built the payout and reconciliation software that roughly 140 mid-market retail chains across India used to pay their vendors — apparel wholesalers, packaging suppliers, cold-chain logistics firms — through a single bank-integrated rail. The platform moved about ₹6 crore a day in vendor payouts. Three weeks earlier, the Reserve Bank of India had issued a revised reconciliation timeline for bulk payout batches above a stated threshold, requiring structured remittance data and same-day matching from 1 April 2026. Kavya's team had exactly three working weeks to ship a new CSV bulk-upload module before that date, and no margin for a second attempt.

The team was small: two backend engineers, one QA analyst, and an AI coding assistant the engineers used daily to turn specifications into working modules — writing the validation logic, the batch-execution service, and the reconciliation matcher from natural-language instructions rather than hand-typing every line. Kavya had written what she considered a complete product requirements document: eleven pages, three user stories, a data dictionary, and a paragraph describing the bulk-upload flow. One of her engineers, Rohan, had taken that paragraph, pasted it more or less verbatim into the assistant, and generated a working first version overnight. It compiled. It ran. In the demo that Monday it handled a clean sample file beautifully. What Kavya was looking at on Tuesday morning was QA's list of everything the generated module got wrong once real data touched it: duplicate vendor IDs silently overwriting each other, a negative payout amount accepted without complaint, a file with a stray currency symbol in one cell crashing the whole batch instead of flagging one row, and no behaviour at all specified for a partially failed batch — the exact scenario the new RBI rule existed to catch. Seven defects, each discovered late, each requiring a design decision Kavya thought she had already made in her head but had never written down anywhere the builder could see.

The question in front of her was not whether to use the AI builder — that decision had been made months earlier — and not whether her spec was thorough by the usual standards of a PRD, because by those standards it was. The question was narrower and sharper: what, exactly, separates an instruction detailed enough for a human colleague to infer the missing pieces from an instruction precise enough that a builder — which does not infer, does not share her assumptions, and does not know what she left out — builds what she actually meant. Three weeks, ₹6 crore a day in payouts, and a regulator's deadline turned that question from an academic one into the single highest-leverage thing Kavya could do that week.

The idea: a prompt is not a description, it is a contract

Prompting a builder from a spec is the practice of translating a product specification — written for human readers who fill gaps with judgment and shared context — into an instruction precise and complete enough that a builder with no access to that judgment or context produces the intended result on or near the first attempt. The "builder" can be a human engineer, but the practice earned its name and its urgency once AI coding assistants made it possible to go from a paragraph of English to running code in minutes, which meant the cost of an imprecise instruction stopped being absorbed by a human engineer's common sense and started showing up directly in the output.

The problem this discipline was invented to solve is an old one wearing new clothes. Product requirements documents have always had implicit content — assumptions the author never wrote down because she assumed the reader would supply them from experience, from the codebase, from last week's stand-up conversation. A capable human engineer supplies that missing context automatically, often without noticing he is doing it; he has seen a hundred bulk-upload features before and knows, without being told, that duplicate IDs need a rule and that partial failure needs a defined behaviour. An AI builder supplies nothing it was not given. It has seen many bulk-upload features in its training data too, but it has no way of knowing which of its many plausible guesses matches the one Kavya had in mind, so it picks one — usually the simplest, most common pattern — and builds that instead. The gap between what was written and what was meant, which a human engineer used to close for free, now surfaces as a defect.

The practice does not have a single named inventor. It crystallised as engineering teams working with GPT-3-and-later coding assistants from roughly 2021 onward — first as line-completion tools, then, from about 2023, as agentic builders capable of writing and wiring up entire modules from a natural-language brief — discovered empirically that the same paragraph handed to two different builders, or the same builder twice, could produce meaningfully different code, and that the variance shrank sharply once the instruction stopped describing intent in prose and started specifying it as an explicit, checkable contract. What crystallised was less a new idea than an old discipline — the behaviour-driven development habit of writing acceptance criteria before code, familiar to product managers as "given/when/then" — rediscovered as mandatory rather than optional, because the reader had changed. The sentence Kavya could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: a builder builds what the prompt says, not what the spec meant, so the prompt has to say all of it.

Figure 1. A spec-to-prompt translation is not one sentence expanded into a longer sentence; it is seven distinct components, several of which a PRD written for humans never states because a human reader is expected to supply them. The review step closes the loop against the same acceptance criteria the prompt stated — not against whether the demo looked right.

How the translation actually works

The mechanics sound almost too simple stated abstractly, which is exactly why they are skipped under deadline pressure. Kavya's team, once they slowed down enough to name the steps, found six of them, and three were things Rohan had genuinely never thought to write down before that week.

The first step is separating the spec's narrative from its rules. A PRD tells a story — a retailer's finance team uploads a file, the system validates it, payouts execute — and stories are exactly what a human reader needs to build a mental model, but a builder does not need the story; it needs the rules embedded inside the story pulled out and made explicit. The second step, and the one most often skipped, is writing the data contract literally: not "a CSV of vendor payments" but the exact column names, types, which are required, what a valid vendor ID looks like, and what currency and amount format is expected — because "a CSV of vendor payments" is a sentence a human fills in from having seen a hundred CSVs, and a builder fills in from having seen a different hundred, matching neither Panchali's bank nor its retailers' export format. The third step is stating constraints as limits, not aspirations: not "the system should handle large files" but "must accept files up to 50,000 rows and reject, not silently truncate, anything larger." The fourth step, the one Kavya's PRD had entirely skipped, is enumerating edge cases by name and pairing each with the expected behaviour — not "handle errors gracefully" but a numbered list: duplicate vendor ID in the same file, negative or zero amount, missing bank IFSC code, a row with more columns than the header, a file where every row fails validation, a file where some rows fail and others succeed. The fifth step is acceptance criteria written as pass/fail statements a QA analyst — or the builder itself, in a self-check pass — could evaluate without asking Kavya what she meant. The sixth and last step, the one practitioners most often leave implicit because it feels unnecessary, is stating non-goals: telling the builder explicitly that this module does not need to support recurring payout schedules or multi-currency conversion yet, because without that sentence a capable builder sometimes builds the more general, more impressive version nobody asked for and nobody has time to review.

Once those six steps are done, the actual prompt is closer to a structured brief than a paragraph: a short role and context statement, the objective, the data contract, the constraints, the enumerated edge cases with one worked negative example showing a wrong output and why it is wrong, the acceptance criteria, and the non-goals. What changes is not the amount of thinking Kavya has to do — she already knew, in her head, what a duplicate vendor ID should do — but where that thinking lives. Before, it lived in her head and in a Slack thread from three months ago. After, it lives in the artifact the builder actually reads.

The arithmetic of an unwritten edge case

Kavya's team kept defect data in Jira from the previous two quarters, and it gave her a number she could use rather than argue from intuition: correcting a defect discovered after generation — deciding the missing rule, changing the code, and re-testing — cost an average of 3.5 engineer-hours per case, almost all of it spent re-establishing context rather than typing. That number let her turn Tuesday's seven defects into an argument rather than a complaint.

The original bulk-upload feature had nine known edge cases, drawn from QA's list and Kavya's own review of three months of support tickets from a comparable feature. Rohan's original prompt — the eleven-page PRD's paragraph, pasted in — stated none of them explicitly; the builder inferred behaviour from patterns common in the training data it had seen, which happened to cover two of the nine correctly by coincidence: it rejected an empty file and it handled a missing header row. That is 2 of 9, or 22 percent, covered on the first pass, leaving 7 missed. At 3.5 hours per missed case, the rework bill was 7 × 3.5 = 24.5 engineer-hours — over three working days for a two-person backend team already down to fifteen working days before the deadline.

Kavya rewrote the prompt using the six-step translation above: nine edge cases named individually, each paired with an expected behaviour, and one negative example showing the exact wrong output the first generation had produced for a duplicate vendor ID, labelled as wrong. Rohan ran the new prompt against the same builder. This time it covered 8 of the 9 edge cases correctly on the first pass — 89 percent — missing only the partial-batch-failure case, which needed a follow-up clarification about whether partially failed batches should auto-retry or hold for manual release. Missed cases: 1. Rework: 1 × 3.5 = 3.5 engineer-hours. The saving from rewriting the prompt, on this one feature, was 24.5 minus 3.5, or 21 engineer-hours — roughly two and a half working days recovered, which was the entire margin the team had against the RBI deadline. At Panchali's loaded cost of roughly ₹1,800 an hour for a senior backend engineer in Bengaluru, that is close to ₹37,800 saved on rework for a single feature, before counting the schedule risk avoided.

Ambiguous (PRD paragraph, pasted in)92 (22%)724.544,100
Structured (six-step translation)98 (89%)13.56,300

The second pass tests whether that arithmetic holds when the input changes, because a result that only works at one scale is not a lesson, it is an anecdote. Two weeks later, Panchali's largest client asked for the same bulk-upload module to also support partial refunds and payouts in two currencies for cross-border vendors, which raised the count of known edge cases from 9 to 20 — duplicate handling now had to interact with currency, refunds had to interact with the reconciliation matcher, and so on. Kavya re-ran both styles of prompt as a controlled comparison before committing to the approach for the expanded scope. The ambiguous style did not merely fail to scale, it degraded: with more implicit decisions for the builder to guess at once, its coverage fell to roughly 15 percent, or 3 of 20 cases, leaving 17 missed and 17 × 3.5 = 59.5 hours of rework — nearly a full sprint for two engineers. The structured style held up better but not perfectly: listing twenty edge cases instead of nine introduced one transcription slip of its own, so coverage came in at 85 percent, 17 of 20, with 3 missed and 3 × 3.5 = 10.5 hours of rework. The gap between the two approaches, which was 21 hours at the smaller scope, widened to 49 hours at the larger one. The lesson Kavya drew from the second pass was not that precise prompting is nice to have; it was that the value of precision compounds with complexity, because ambiguity does not fail gracefully — it fails in proportion to how much the builder is left to guess.

Figure 2. The gap between an ambiguous and a structured prompt is 21 hours at nine known edge cases and 49 hours at twenty. Precision does not save a fixed amount of rework; it saves a growing share of it as the feature gets more complex.

Eight distinctions worth sitting with

Precise is not the same as complete

A prompt can specify a narrow slice of behaviour with total precision and still be wrong, because it precisely describes the wrong scope. Kavya's second-pass prompt was more precise per edge case than her first, but if she had precisely specified nine edge cases while missing that eleven existed, precision would have bought her nothing. Precision is a property of each statement in the prompt; completeness is a property of the whole. A learner who conflates them starts polishing sentences before checking whether the list of things being polished is the right list.

The builder is not deterministic, so the prompt cannot be trusted alone

The same structured prompt, run twice against the same builder, can produce two different implementations of the same rule — one that rejects a duplicate vendor ID with an error message, another that silently keeps the first occurrence. Both may satisfy a loosely worded acceptance criterion. This is why acceptance criteria have to be specific enough to fail one of those two outputs, and why a single successful generation is evidence, not proof, that the prompt worked — a point returned to below under common mistakes.

A PRD register and a prompt register are different languages

A PRD is written to be read by a person who will ask a clarifying question if confused. A prompt is written to be read by something that will not ask, and will instead proceed confidently on its best guess. The habit of writing PRDs — narrative, motivational, building a case for why the feature matters — actively works against prompting a builder well, because narrative buries the rules the builder needs inside sentences optimised for human persuasion rather than machine precision.

Telling the builder what versus how

Over-specifying implementation — naming the exact library, function, or algorithm — can constrain a builder away from a better solution it would otherwise have found, and it signals a kind of false confidence: Kavya is a product manager, not a backend engineer, and instructing the builder to use a specific database index strategy is a decision she is not well placed to make. The discipline is to specify the what — the contract, the constraint, the observable behaviour — and leave the how to the builder and the engineer reviewing it, intervening on implementation only where a real constraint (cost, latency, an existing system it must integrate with) makes the how a business decision in disguise.

What the builder can see at once has a limit

A builder working from a prompt has a bounded context window — a ceiling on how much text it can hold in working memory at one time — and pasting an entire eleven-page PRD into that window does not make the builder better informed; it makes the rules that matter compete for attention with narrative that does not. The discipline is to extract the relevant contract and constraints into the prompt itself and reference supporting material rather than dumping it wholesale, the same way a good manager briefs a new hire on the two things that matter for today's task rather than handing over the entire onboarding wiki.

This is not "prompt engineering" as trick-finding

The term prompt engineering often connotes finding a clever phrase or incantation that happens to produce better output — a magic word. Prompting a builder from a spec is closer to the opposite: it is applying the same rigor a good engineering manager already applies to writing acceptance criteria for a human engineer, made mandatory because the reader no longer forgives vagueness with inference. A PM who already writes precise, testable acceptance criteria is most of the way there; a PM chasing a clever phrasing is solving the wrong problem.

It cannot tell you whether you are building the right thing

However precisely Kavya specifies the bulk-upload module, precision only governs whether the builder constructs what she described — it says nothing about whether the feature she described is the one her retailers actually need, or whether the RBI deadline might be better met with a narrower interim fix than a full module. Prompting discipline answers "will the builder build what I meant," not "did I mean the right thing." Those are different questions, and conflating them is a common trap: a beautifully specified feature that solves the wrong problem is still the wrong problem, built faster.

It works badly on problems you have not yet explored

The whole practice assumes the acceptance criteria are knowable in advance. On a genuinely exploratory problem — where Kavya does not yet know what "correct" looks like because no one has used the feature yet — writing a precise, locked-down prompt too early forces a premature answer into the builder's output before the team has learned enough to know what the right answer is. In that situation, a rougher, more exploratory generation, followed by observation, is the better tool; precise prompting is for well-understood problems with discoverable edge cases, not for problems still being discovered.

Where the picture changes: product type and company stage

The mechanics above hold everywhere, but what belongs in the prompt shifts with what kind of product is being built and how large the company behind it is. A consumer product's prompts lean heavily on behavioural and visual acceptance criteria — how a screen should feel under a slow network, what an empty state should say — criteria that are harder to write as crisp pass/fail statements than a B2B data contract is, which is why consumer teams more often pair a prompt with an example screenshot or reference flow rather than trying to describe the feel in words alone. A B2B platform like Panchali leans the other way: its prompts are dominated by data contracts, role and permission rules, audit-trail requirements, and integration constraints with a client's own systems, because the cost of an unstated business rule shows up as an incorrect payment rather than an awkward screen. A marketplace product adds a further twist — its prompts must specify behaviour on both sides of a transaction at once, and its hardest edge cases live at the seam between them, such as what happens when a seller cancels an order after a buyer has already paid, a case neither a pure buyer-side nor pure seller-side spec would surface on its own.

Company stage matters just as much as product type. At an early-stage company, the product manager often is the one typing the prompt directly into the builder with no engineer standing between the spec and the code, which makes prompting literacy a personal, immediate survival skill — the cost of Kavya's own imprecision would have landed on her own week, not a team's. At a larger, more mature company, the prompt itself tends to become an institutional artifact: reviewed by a platform team for architectural fit, checked by a security function for data-handling constraints, and stored alongside the ticket for traceability, because a large organisation cannot rely on any one person's memory of what was meant — the prompt has to survive being read by someone who was not in the room when it was written.

Table 2. What changes in a builder prompt across product type and company stage.
ContextWhat the prompt must carry more of
Consumer productBehavioural and visual acceptance criteria; reference examples, since feel is hard to state in words alone
B2B platformData contracts, permission rules, audit trail and integration constraints with client systems
MarketplaceTwo-sided behaviour and seam cases at the interaction between buyer and seller, or supply and demand
Early-stage companyNothing extra structurally, but the PM often writes it directly — precision is a personal survival skill
Large companyInstitutional traceability — the prompt as a reviewed artifact others must be able to read cold

Where this goes wrong, three ways

The first common mistake is pasting the narrative spec straight into the builder, exactly as Rohan did on the first attempt. The symptom is a generation that handles the obvious happy path beautifully and nothing else, because the underlying misunderstanding treats "detailed" and "precise" as synonyms — an eleven-page PRD feels thorough to the person who wrote it, but thoroughness for a human reader and precision for a builder are not the same property. The cheapest diagnostic is to hand the prompt, not the PRD, to a colleague who knows nothing about the feature and ask her to state back the five most important rules; if she cannot, neither could the builder.

The second mistake is specifying only the happy path and trusting the builder — or oneself — to infer the rest, which is what produced Kavya's first-pass 22 percent coverage. The underlying misunderstanding is treating "what usually happens" as if it were the whole specification, when in most real features the edge cases outnumber the happy path and carry most of the risk. The cheapest diagnostic is arithmetic rather than instinct: count the known edge cases from past tickets or support data, count how many the prompt names explicitly, and treat anything under roughly half as a rework bill waiting to be discovered by QA instead of by the prompt.

The third mistake is treating one successful generation as proof the prompt worked, which matters because builders are not deterministic and a demo that looks clean can still be a coincidence. The symptom is code that works in the walkthrough and breaks in production on a case nobody happened to test during the demo. The cheapest diagnostic is to re-run the same prompt two or three times and compare the outputs; if the implementations differ materially between runs, the acceptance criteria were not specific enough to pin the behaviour down, no matter how good any single run looked.

A fourth, quieter mistake is over-specifying the how — naming a particular library, data structure, or algorithm out of habit or a desire to sound technically credible — which produces code that is brittle or inefficient because it followed a literal instruction instead of the engineer's better judgment on implementation. The symptom shows up in code review as a raised eyebrow from the engineer rather than a functional bug, and the diagnostic is a simple test: for every implementation detail in the prompt, ask whether it is really a business constraint in disguise (must integrate with an existing system, must meet a latency limit) or just a habit; if it is a habit, cut it.

"A builder builds what the prompt says, not what the spec meant — so the prompt has to say all of it."

What good looked like, three weeks later

By 27 March, four days ahead of the RBI deadline, the bulk-upload module Kavya's team shipped looked, from the outside, unremarkable — which was the point. The prompt that produced its final version ran to about a page and a half: two sentences of role and context, one sentence naming the objective as a result rather than a task, an explicit data contract with every column and type named, four numbered constraints including the 50,000-row ceiling, all eleven edge cases by then identified (the original nine plus two more QA had found while testing the structured version) each paired with an expected behaviour, one negative example showing the exact wrong output the first, ambiguous-prompt attempt had produced weeks earlier so the builder would not repeat it, nine acceptance criteria written as statements a person could check without asking Kavya anything, and two explicit non-goals ruling out recurring schedules and further currency support for this release. Rohan ran it, reviewed the output against each acceptance criterion individually rather than by eyeballing the demo, found one criterion failing on a boundary condition at exactly 50,000 rows, fixed that one item, and re-ran the check — not the whole generation. Total rework on the final version: under two hours. The team had time left over to add a manual-release option for partially failed batches, a refinement nobody had asked for and Kavya would not have had the days to consider if the first three weeks had gone the way the first attempt suggested they would.

What Kavya decided, and what to learn next

Kavya's decision, once she had the Tuesday-morning numbers in front of her, was not to abandon the AI builder or to write even longer PRDs; it was to separate the two documents entirely — the PRD would stay a narrative artifact for stakeholders, and a distinct, shorter prompt artifact, built from the six-step translation, would become the thing actually handed to the builder and reviewed line by line against acceptance criteria before anything shipped. The reasoning was the arithmetic itself: 21 hours saved at the feature's original scope, 49 hours saved once scope grew, against a deadline that had no slack for either. The one-page prompt cost her perhaps ninety extra minutes to write over the paragraph Rohan had pasted in originally; it returned multiple days.

The natural next thing to learn, once this discipline is comfortable, is how to treat the spec itself as a prompt for an AI builder from the start — designing the specification document so that its structure already matches what a builder needs, rather than writing a PRD and then separately translating it — which collapses two documents into one without losing precision. Closely behind that sits the harder skill this one depends on: reviewing work a PM did not write and cannot read line by line, since the entire value of precise prompting evaporates if nobody checks the output against the criteria that were written down. Two questions worth sitting with before moving on: when a generated feature passes its demo cleanly, what is the cheapest way to tell whether that is because the prompt was precise or because the demo simply never exercised the cases that would have exposed an ambiguity; and for a feature not yet built where the right behaviour is still genuinely unknown, how would a PM know she is in that situation rather than one where the edge cases are knowable and she has simply not yet done the work of naming them?

Two questions to sit with.
1. When a generated feature passes its demo cleanly, what is the cheapest way to tell whether that happened because the prompt was precise, or because the demo never touched the cases that would have exposed an ambiguity?
2. For a feature whose right behaviour is still genuinely unknown, how does a PM recognise that she is in exploratory territory rather than simply not yet having done the work of naming the edge cases?

Rakam Wealth Technologies: Writing the Withdrawal

An ambiguous case in Delivery & Technology · Technical Fluency

1. Indiranagar, Wednesday night

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Wednesday 21 October 2026, Chandrani Jayadevan, director of product, was still at her dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with three documents open and the ceiling fan on low. The first was a one-page prompt she had written that afternoon. The second was a fourteen-page draft specification somebody else had written for the same feature. The third was a spreadsheet of 2,340 rows that she had been told, nine days earlier, was not reliable.

At eleven the next morning she had to tell the steering group how Rakam Wealth Technologies would build self-serve partial withdrawal: the screen on which an investor using a distributor's app asks for part of her money back from a mutual fund scheme, sees what the exit load will take, and confirms. The contract with Raqeem Wealth Partners in Dubai put the feature live on Tuesday 1 December 2026. Most of the code would be written by an AI coding assistant, from instructions Chandrani would be responsible for. The assistant was fast, patient and literal. Where the instruction was silent it did not stop; it chose, and what it chose looked like working software.

The question on the table was not whether to use the assistant. The question was how much of the rule set to write down before letting it start, in what form, and who would decide the rules that nobody at Rakam agreed on.

2. How Rakam came to be built this way

Rakam was founded in 2019 by Chidvilas Jithendran and two colleagues from a Bengaluru brokerage. It does not hold money and does not advise. It sells white-label transaction infrastructure to mutual fund distributors: the order-placement rails, the folio views, the mandate plumbing and the statements that sit inside a distributor's own app. By October 2026 it served 41 independent distributors and two bank clients, covering 18.6 lakh investor accounts and about ₹24,800 crore of assets, on revenue of ₹96 crore in FY2026.

The decision that shapes today was taken in the second half of 2023. To win its first bank client, Rakam promised a six-week white-label launch. A rules service — one machine-readable place where each scheme's exit load, lock-in and rounding convention lived — was costed at eleven weeks. Chidvilas chose instead to let each distributor keep its own configuration sheet, uploaded nightly, and to read scheme terms from the registrar feeds alongside it. The bank went live in seven weeks. Three years later there are 41 configuration sheets, two registrar feeds, and no single authority on what an exit load is. Every later product has paid rent on that choice, and a prompt is the first thing that cannot pretend otherwise: a specification can point at a rules table only if a rules table exists.

3. The industry

Indian mutual fund distribution has been pulled in two directions for a decade. At one end, direct platforms — Zerodha Coin, Groww, Paytm Money, PhonePe — teach retail investors to transact without an intermediary, and have made a clean withdrawal screen table stakes. At the other, the AMFI-registered distributor channel still carries the bulk of regular-plan assets, and those distributors buy their technology rather than build it. Rakam sells to the second group and is judged by the first group's screens.

The constraints are real and external. SEBI's distribution rules mean Rakam's screens may inform but not recommend, so a withdrawal screen cannot suggest an amount. Unit and load data come from the registrars, CAMS and KFintech, on their schedules. Mandates run on NPCI's UPI AutoPay rails. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs what Rakam may show about an investor's holdings and to whom, and platform fees carry 18 per cent GST. Rakam's exposure is also global: Raqeem in Dubai serves 46,000 non-resident investors, and Clarence Johnson is selling the same rails to NRI channels out of New Jersey. A withdrawal flow built for Indiranagar is signed off in the DIFC.

4. The situation in detail

Rakam licensed the coding assistant in June 2026 and shipped four modules with it (Exhibit 1). The first, nominee update, was prompted in 240 words and came back with eleven defects in user-acceptance testing. The conclusion drawn in July was that the prompt had been too short. In August the bank-mandate re-registration module was prompted in 1,980 words with nine worked examples and came back with four defects, which the engineering team read as confirmation. In September the capital-gains statement module was prompted in 1,310 words — the second-longest prompt written — with no examples, and came back with twelve.

Two of those beliefs have since weakened. The mandate module was the only one whose rules already existed in machine-readable form outside Rakam, in NPCI's published mandate specification; its prompt, its examples and its source of truth all changed together. And when Cyriac Joseph's team classified the twelve capital-gains defects in early October, six of them sat on rules the prompt had stated — stated in a sentence that admitted two readings.

Then the ground moved under the rules themselves. On 12 October an audit by the Pune team compared the 41 distributor configuration sheets against the registrar feeds for every scheme-plan combination live on the platform. Of 2,340 rows, 417 disagreed, 17.8 per cent of the book. Of those 417, 138 differed only in the date from which a load took effect; the remaining 279 differed in the load itself. Nobody has established which side is right, and the distributors who maintain the sheets are the customers who pay. Exhibit 2 describes the resulting exceptions in September, twice, from two systems that do not agree either.

5. The people

Chidvilas Jithendran, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru, wants the rules expressed as executable test fixtures rather than prose, and the builder made to pass them. He also authored the 2023 configuration-sheet decision, is raising a Series C in the first quarter of 2027, and has not said that a rules service would now take the eleven weeks he cannot spare.

Cyriac Joseph, engineering lead, Pune, must sign off whatever the assistant produces. Four of his nine engineers are on a bank migration until 6 November. He argues for the full written specification because his team cannot review code against intentions nobody recorded. What he does not say in meetings is that his best reviewer has resigned, with a last working day of 20 November.

Chhanda Jaleel, product designer, Berlin, holds that whatever the builder generates becomes the product, because nobody redesigns a screen that already works. She wants the flow designed before it is prompted. Her incentive is a design system she is trying to make load-bearing; she has not mentioned that she is on leave from 2 to 6 November.

Chanakya Jagathy, data scientist, Toronto, built the log classifier behind the second half of Exhibit 2 and the forecast behind Exhibit 4. He wants worked examples drawn from real transactions and has twice asked what else changed between the four modules in Exhibit 1. He has not volunteered that his classifier was recalibrated on 20 October and that September's figures moved.

Celestine Jacobkutty, customer-success lead, Singapore, absorbs every exception at 06:30 IST before the Indian desks open. She wants the write path delayed and only an estimate shipped, because her queue is staffed for 1,284 tickets a month, not for what a wrong load would produce. She has not said that two of her four analysts are contractors ending in December.

Clarence Johnson, sales head, New Jersey, has sold the withdrawal flow into three NRI channel conversations for a January campaign and treats 1 December as immovable. His variable pay sits on signed, not shipped. He has not told Chandrani that Raqeem's head of digital asked him, on 14 October, whether a read-only estimate would satisfy the contract.

Exhibit 6 is the options table Chandrani will put on the screen at eleven.

7. Voices

“I can review a diff against a sentence. I cannot review a diff against a mood. Give me the fourteen pages and I will sign; give me a paragraph and my team becomes the specification, after the fact, at midnight.”Cyriac Joseph, engineering review call, 19 October
“Prose is where rules go to be misread. Sixty fixtures with inputs and exact outputs and the builder has nowhere to be creative. And before anyone asks: yes, I know who wrote the config sheets in 2023.”Chidvilas Jithendran, same call
“Where do the sixty examples come from? If they come from production they encode the load values in the sheets, and 417 of those rows are disputed. We would be teaching the builder the argument instead of settling it.”Chanakya Jagathy, chat thread, 20 October, 21:48 IST
“Nobody writes the empty state, the error copy or the confirmation into a rules document, and then nobody redesigns them. Whatever it generates on 12 November is what 18.6 lakh people will read in January.”Chhanda Jaleel, email, 20 October
“Thirty per cent of my tickets are load disputes today, before we let investors do this themselves. Ship the estimate, keep the request with us, and I will stop arguing about prompts altogether.”Celestine Jacobkutty, Singapore, 21 October, 07:10 IST
“Twenty lakh a month against a credit capped at twenty-four lakh once. The build costs seven and a half. So what exactly are we protecting by waiting, and what do I tell three channels in January?”Clarence Johnson, call with Chandrani, 21 October, 20:30 IST

8. The options as Chandrani sees them

Option A, the full prose specification. Ten days of writing with Cyriac's remaining five engineers and Chhanda, producing a document that covers rules, screens and messages and that the team can review against and reuse. Chhanda is on leave for five of the ten writing days. Cyriac's best reviewer leaves on 20 November, after three of the five review days.

Option B, rules plus executable examples. One page of rules the builder cannot infer, and 60 worked examples with exact expected outputs, drawn from September's logs. It is the cheapest and the earliest of the three building options, and it has the longest margin of the three. It also requires somebody to state a load value for every disputed scheme-plan row an example touches, which is the decision nobody has taken.

Option C, thin prompt and hardening. Start on Monday with one page, let the assistant produce something by Friday, then spend ten days reviewing behaviour rather than code. It needs the most reviewer time in the fortnight when Berlin has fallen to 5.5 hours of overlap and Toronto to none (Exhibit 5).

Option D, estimate only. Ship a read-only screen that shows what a withdrawal would cost and routes the request to Celestine's desk, deferring the write path to the first quarter of 2027. Whether it discharges the Raqeem obligation is a question Clarence has already been asked and has not relayed, and Celestine's queue absorbs the volume Exhibit 4 prices.

Across the bottom of the printed table Chandrani had written: “none of these rows decides the 417, and none of them moves where the rules live.”

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The Raqeem master services agreement puts self-serve withdrawal live on 1 December 2026, with service credits of ₹6 lakh for each completed week of delay, capped at ₹24 lakh. Rakam's own code freeze runs from 18 December to 1 January, so anything not shipped by 17 December waits for January. Of the FY2027 product budget, ₹1.62 crore remained on 1 October; every option in Exhibit 6 fits inside it several times over. People are the scarce input: five of Cyriac's nine engineers until 6 November, one designer, one data scientist nine and a half hours behind until 1 November and ten and a half after. SEBI's rules forbid the screen from recommending an amount, the DPDP Act governs what may be shown and logged about a holding, and the registrars' feeds arrive when they arrive. A rules service, costed again last week, is eleven weeks of work.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of the four rules in Exhibit 4 could a competent builder infer correctly without being told, and on what basis would you decide that for each one?
  2. What does Exhibit 1 actually establish about prompt length, worked examples and defects, and what would you have to measure to establish the claim the engineering team drew from it in August?
  3. Exhibit 2 reports the same month twice and disagrees with itself. Which column, if either, should Chandrani use to brief the steering group, and what would you do about the other?
  4. Exhibit 4's rows sum to ₹20.33 lakh a month, an upper bound, and the contract caps service credits at ₹24 lakh. What makes those two numbers comparable or not, and which of them should govern the decision?
  5. If the 417 disputed rows cannot be settled before 1 December, what can be specified anyway, and what does the answer imply about where precision is worth paying for?
  6. What should Chandrani do on Monday morning, 26 October, and what should she say to the board in November about how Rakam will instruct a builder from now on?

It was past midnight. Chandrani opened the one-page prompt again and read her own second sentence: the exit load is one per cent of the amount withdrawn. It was one sentence, and she did not know whether it was true for 279 of the 2,340 rows. In six hours Celestine's desk would open in Singapore; in eleven, the steering group. She left the three documents open and turned off the lamp.
case20v1-tech.prompting.builder:
Gandiva Home Services: Writing for a Builder

A decision case in Delivery & Technology

1. The decision

At 6:30 on Monday morning, 19 October 2026, Nithin Yesudas read a message from Toronto and then looked at the calendar. By ten-thirty he had to tell Gandiva Home Services' leadership how the company would build a self-serve reschedule flow for customers. It had to be live by Tuesday 3 November, five days before Diwali on Sunday 8 November.

Most of the build would be done by an AI coding assistant working from a written prompt, and Nithin, group product manager for customer experience, would write it. The assistant is quick and obedient, and also literal: where a prompt is silent, it fills the gap with a guess that looks like working software. The question was not whether to use it. It was how much of the specification to write, in what form, and how much to leave to the builder before the calendar ran out.

2. Company background

Gandiva was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 by two former consultants. It sells services booked to the home (AC servicing, deep-cleaning, appliance repair, plumbing) to urban households in eleven cities, through an app and a call centre. About 6,200 providers are active, mostly self-employed technicians who keep most of each job's price. Gross booking value in FY2026 was ₹420 crore; an average booking is ₹1,750.

The competitive set is familiar: Urban Company at the national top end, and thousands of neighbourhood mechanics reached through WhatsApp and Justdial. Customers pay by UPI, card or cash, and online payments settle through Razorpay. Services carry 18 per cent GST. Since the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Gandiva also treats a customer's phone number as data to be hidden from providers until a job is confirmed. Diwali is the sharpest peak of the year, because households clean before Lakshmi puja.

3. The situation

Today a customer who wants to move a booking must phone support. In September, 9 per cent of bookings were rescheduled. For the fortnight from 3 November the company forecasts 3,90,000 bookings, so about 35,100 rescheduled bookings if September's rate holds, which we treat as one request each, and support wants them self-served.

The rules look simple. Rescheduling is free until four hours before the slot. Inside four hours the customer pays a fee of 20 per cent of booking value, ₹350 on an average booking, unless the provider caused the delay. Over the last eight weeks, 12 per cent of reschedule requests fell inside the four-hour window. At forecast volume that is 4,212 requests; if the fee were wrongly waived on every one, the leakage would be 4,212 × ₹350 = ₹14.74 lakh.

The team saw the problem from different places. In Pune, engineers worried about reviewing generated code in the last fortnight before a festival. In Toronto, Navin pointed out that the four-hour window, though only 12 per cent of requests, was where every rupee of fee revenue arose. In Berlin, Nikhila saw the reschedule screen as a trust moment, when a customer deciding whether to keep a stranger's visit to her home decides again.

Nithin's first draft prompt was one paragraph. Neethu Yermal, his engineering lead in Pune, listed what it left unsaid: whether 20 per cent applies before or after a coupon, whether the ₹350 includes GST, what "provider caused the delay" means, and whether a booking can be moved twice. Each was a place where a builder would guess. Exhibit 1 shows what guessing had already cost on three earlier internal tools.

4. The people

Neethu Yermal, engineering lead, Pune. She must review and sign off whatever the builder produces. She wants a complete written specification to review against, and fears her team becoming reviewers of code nobody explained. She leans towards a full specification, and has said so.

Navin Yohannan, data scientist, Toronto. He owns the September numbers. Toronto is 9.5 hours behind India until 1 November, so his notes arrived at 9 pm Sunday, 6:30 am Monday in Bengaluru. He wants eight real cases from the logs used as worked examples in the prompt, and argues that the four-hour window is where the money is.

Nikhila Yellur, designer, Berlin. Her morning starts at 12:30 pm IST until the clocks change on 25 October. She wants her screens designed first, since a builder's default layout will be what customers see if nobody intervenes, and she resists anything that cuts her out. Berlin falls to 4.5 hours behind India after the clocks change, so her overlap with Bengaluru shrinks by an hour from 26 October, just when reviews begin.

5. Exhibits

In Exhibit 1 the longest prompt matched intent on 9 of 11 behaviours, but it was also the only one with several worked examples. Three attempts cannot separate length from examples, and the tools differ, but rework fell as examples rose: 6, 3, then 2 days.

Exhibit 2 puts the dates on one line. Whichever option is chosen, the work lands between 27 and 30 October, and the go-live date does not move: Diwali-week bookings open on 3 November whether or not the flow is ready. The distance from each ready marker to 3 November is the margin that absorbs a failed review.

6. The options

Exhibit 3 sets the three courses against the calendar of Exhibit 2.

Option A: a short prompt, then iterate. Nithin states the rules in one paragraph and lets the assistant start on Monday. The upside is speed and no demand on Neethu's team before the build. The cost is Exhibit 1's first row: if this behaves like that attempt, rework is six days, and the build is ready on 28 October with three spare days (Exhibit 3). Every unstated rule is a guess in production, and the fee leakage above, at most ₹14.74 lakh, is its visible price. Navin expects the fee base to be the first rule guessed wrong.

Option B: a full specification first. Neethu's team and Nikhila write a fourteen-page document covering rules, screens and messages, with five worked examples. The upside is completeness and a document the team can review against and reuse. The cost is five days of writing before anything is built, one spare day, and a document that may be wrong in places nobody tests until the end. It also pulls Neethu and Nikhila off their own work for the whole of the first week.

Option C: a precise one-page rules prompt. Nithin writes only what the builder cannot know: the fee base, GST treatment, the definition of provider delay, move limits and phone masking, with eight worked examples from Navin's logs. Layout and copy are left to the builder inside Nikhila's design frame. The upside is four spare days. The cost is that anything not written is still guessed, and the gaps will show first in screens and wording.

Exhibit 3. Working days from Monday 19 October. 7. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of the reschedule rules could the builder safely infer, and which could it only guess? How would you sort them?
  2. What do the three rows of Exhibit 1 show, and what can they not show about prompt length against worked examples?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, what does each option buy with its spare days, and whose time does each one spend?
  4. Which option would you take to the ten-thirty meeting, and what would you check on 27 October before agreeing to go live?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision as one question: where does a wrong guess cost more than a sentence? Precision is worth spending on facts only the company knows (fee base, GST treatment, what counts as provider delay), on consequences in law or money (the DPDP masking rule, the leakage bound), and on anything the builder cannot see. It is not worth spending on taste, such as layout or wording, which is cheap to look at and cheap to change.

One defensible path is Option C. Nithin fixes the fee as 20 per cent of the price shown at booking, before coupons, GST included, and writes eight worked examples, each with inputs and exact expected outputs, so the examples act as both specification and test. He asks the builder to restate the rules and list its assumptions before writing code, runs the eight examples before anyone looks at a screen, and invites Neethu to review the rules rather than all the code. Nikhila supplies the design frame; the builder fills it. Navin's examples give the prompt its evidence.

The reasoning rests on Exhibits 1 and 3. Examples were the variable that tracked with fewer unmatched behaviours and less rework, and C converts the saved days into a margin that absorbs a failed 27 October review. Option B is defensible if the spec will outlive this build. Option A is not, because its saving is the one that can cost ₹14.74 lakh in a single fortnight.

Prompting a Builder from a Spec

Precision is not a virtue you add to an instruction; it is a quantity you spend, unevenly, on the few decisions where the builder's guess and your intention are most likely to diverge and most expensive when they do. This page is about how experienced practitioners decide where to spend it — and about the three or four serious positions they hold, which do not reconcile.

1. Two rooms, three weeks apart

On the afternoon of 14 May 2026, Ira Bhattacharya, vice-president of product at Shabdika Speech Cloud in Pune, sat in a review she had called herself and could not get a straight answer out of. Shabdika sold an Indian-language voice agent that handled inbound calls for banks, insurers and two large hospital chains — roughly 2.1 million calls a month across nine languages, with the agent authorised to do real work on the caller's account: check a claim status, reissue a policy document, schedule a callback. The agent's usefulness lived in a layer the team called tool-calling: the model decided, mid-conversation, which backend operation to invoke and with what arguments. Ira's team had rebuilt that layer over eleven days using an AI coding assistant, and the rebuild was, by every measure the engineers cared about, a success. It was 40 per cent faster, the code was cleaner, the test suite was green.

What Ira could not get an answer to was a customer complaint from a general insurer in Mumbai: on about one call in three hundred, the agent had begun reading back a policy number that belonged to a different policy held by the same customer. Nobody had asked for that behaviour. Nobody had forbidden it either. Buried in the generated code was a helper that, when a lookup returned more than one matching policy, selected the most recently updated one and proceeded without asking the caller to disambiguate. It was a perfectly defensible engineering decision. It was also, under the insurer's own compliance policy and under the disclosure norms the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India expects of intermediaries, the wrong one. The specification Ira's team had handed the builder said, in full, "look up the caller's policy and confirm the details before proceeding." Six of the eleven words in that sentence were doing work. The word the was carrying a uniqueness assumption that had been true in the test fixtures and was false for about 8 per cent of the insurer's book.

Three weeks later and six hundred kilometres south, on 2 June 2026, Karthik Subramanian faced a version of the same problem with the opposite physics. Karthik was general manager for product at Shilpan Instruments in Coimbatore, which made cold-chain telemetry — a battery-powered logger that rode inside refrigerated pharmaceutical vehicles, sampled temperature and door state, and uplinked over cellular to a dashboard that Shilpan's customers, mostly pharmaceutical distributors, used to prove to auditors that a consignment had never left its permitted range. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation's expectations around distribution practice meant that an unproven excursion was, commercially, the same as a spoiled consignment: the stock was written off. Shilpan's three largest customers moved between ₹4 crore and ₹11 crore of temperature-sensitive stock a month each.

Karthik's team was rewriting the alerting service — the cloud component that turned a stream of readings into excursion events, notifications and the daily compliance report. They were using the same class of AI builder that Shabdika used. The difference was that half the contract sat in firmware on 34,000 devices already in the field, where a mistake could not be hot-fixed in an afternoon; devices were reflashed on a service cycle that took, on average, seven months to reach the whole fleet. Beena Thomas, Shilpan's firmware lead in Kochi, had written the device side four years earlier and had made a decision that was entirely sensible at the time: the logger reported temperature as a signed integer in tenths of a degree Celsius, to avoid floating point on a small microcontroller. The field in the uplink payload was called temp. The first generation of the new alerting service read that field, compared it against a threshold of 8, and concluded that a vehicle sitting at a comfortable 4.2°C — reported as 42 — had been in excursion for the entire journey. Every consignment on the pilot route was flagged. It took two days to find, because the alerts looked plausible and the logs looked fine.

Both incidents are usually filed under "the spec wasn't detailed enough", which is true and nearly useless. The eleven-word sentence at Shabdika would have passed any PRD review in the country. The Shilpan payload field was documented; the documentation simply lived in a wiki page the builder was never shown. The interesting question, and the one this page is about, is not whether more detail would have helped — more detail always helps, at a price — but which detail, how a practitioner decides in advance where the money should go, and what the serious schools of thought say when they disagree about the answer.

2. The idea, and the four positions people actually hold

Start with a definition precise enough to argue with. A specification does not determine a program; it admits a set of them. Every instruction — a sentence, a PRD, a formal contract — is consistent with many possible implementations, differing in the decisions the instruction did not settle. A builder, whether a human engineer or a language model, selects one member of that admissible set. It does not select at random: it selects according to a prior, learned from everything it has seen before. Prompting a builder from a spec is therefore the practice of shrinking the admissible set, and of shifting the builder's prior within it, in the places where the prior is least likely to land on what you meant. Precision is the mechanism; agreement between the admissible set and the intended set is the goal. The two are not the same thing, and a great deal of confusion follows from treating them as one.

Figure 1. Each layer of an instruction removes candidate programs. The layers are not interchangeable: a data contract with units removes a different class of candidate than a counter-example does, and executable ground truth removes candidates the prose cannot reach because it removes them by test rather than by description. The dashed line is the reminder that narrowing the set does nothing if the intended program was never inside it.

The intellectual history is older than the tools and explains why the disagreements are so stubborn. In 1978 Edsger Dijkstra wrote a short, acid note on what he called the foolishness of natural-language programming, arguing that the imprecision people prize in natural language is exactly what makes it unfit to specify machine behaviour, and that any attempt to program in it would simply relocate the ambiguity rather than remove it. In 1985 Peter Naur published Programming as Theory Building, arguing something almost opposite in spirit: that the real product of programming is a theory held in a person's head about why the system is the way it is, that documentation and specifications are lossy shadows of that theory, and that a program whose theory has been lost cannot be safely modified no matter how good its documentation. Bertrand Meyer's design by contract in the late 1980s gave the specification-first camp a practical vocabulary — preconditions, postconditions, invariants — and behaviour-driven development in the 2000s gave product managers a version of it they could actually write. Fred Brooks, in No Silver Bullet, supplied the sentence that every camp quotes at the others: the hard part of software is deciding what to build, not building it, and tools attack the accidental difficulty while the essential difficulty stays where it was.

There is a fifth ancestor most practitioners have never read and all of them obey. Paul Grice's work on conversational implicature established that cooperative speakers deliberately say less than they mean, because a competent listener is expected to supply the rest, and that saying the obvious is itself a signal that something unusual is going on. Under-specification is not sloppiness; it is a trained reflex of fluent communication, and it is the single hardest habit to unlearn when the listener is a builder that infers from a different corpus of experience than yours. When Ira wrote "the caller's policy", she was being a good Gricean. She was also being wrong.

Out of that history four positions are genuinely held by competent people today. Table 1 states each one as a proposition its adherents would sign and one they would refuse, which is the only honest way to distinguish schools that all describe themselves as pragmatic.

Table 1. Four schools on how to drive a builder from a specification, stated as propositions each would and would not sign.

That you can discover the contract by iterating with the builder — iteration hides which decisions were ever made. Defect-cost curves: rules settled before generation cost minutes, the same rules settled after release cost days.

These are not four flavours of the same advice. The contract-first practitioner and the dialogic practitioner will give opposite instructions on a Monday morning about whether to spend the next two hours writing or generating. The harness practitioner thinks both of them are optimising a channel that does not deserve the attention. The theory-builder thinks all three are measuring the wrong thing. A manager who cannot state which position she is taking, and why, on a particular feature, is not being pragmatic; she is being unexamined.

3. Mechanics in depth: what precision buys, quantitatively

The useful formalism is embarrassingly simple and almost never written down, which is why teams argue about prompting with anecdotes. Treat the unstated content of a specification as a set of decisions d1 … dk that the builder must settle in order to produce running code. For each, let pi be the probability that the builder's prior lands on the branch you intended. Then the probability that a single generation is right in every respect is the product of the pi, and that product is brutal.

Karthik's team, after the temperature incident, went back through the alerting-service prompt and counted the decisions it had left open. There were nineteen: the unit question, the de-duplication window for repeated alerts, what to do when a device clock had drifted, whether raw samples or hourly aggregates were retained, which anomalies counted as an excursion rather than a device fault, the timezone of the daily report, the retry policy for a dropped uplink, and a dozen smaller ones. Assume, generously, that the builder's prior was right 85 per cent of the time on each. Then 0.8519 ≈ 0.046: fewer than one generation in twenty would have been correct everywhere. The team had run three generations and picked the one that looked best, which raises the chance of a clean result to about 13 per cent and does nothing at all to tell you which of the nineteen went wrong in the copy you kept.

Ira ran the same count on the tool-calling layer and found thirty-four open decisions. At a more flattering 90 per cent per decision — the domain is more common in training data than cold-chain telemetry — 0.934 ≈ 0.028. The multi-policy disambiguation was one of the thirty-four, and it was not among the ones anybody worried about.

Figure 2. A per-decision accuracy that sounds excellent in isolation collapses at module scale. At 85 per cent per decision — a builder that "usually gets it right" — a nineteen-decision module has under a 5 per cent chance of being correct throughout. The practical consequence is that the right question is never "will this be right?" but "how many of these will be wrong, and which ones can I afford?"

The compounding curve is arresting but it is not, on its own, actionable, because it argues for specifying everything and everything cannot be specified. The actionable quantity is the expected number of wrong decisions, Σ(1 − pi), and more precisely the expected cost: each decision has a loss Li if the builder gets it wrong and a cost ci to state explicitly. The rule an expert applies, usually without writing it down, is to specify decision i when (1 − pi) · Li > ci. That single inequality dissolves most of the argument between the contract-first and dialogic camps: neither "specify everything" nor "specify nothing and iterate" is right, and the interesting work is estimating three numbers.

Table 2 is the estimate Karthik's team made, in about forty minutes, for the ten most consequential open decisions in the alerting service. The numbers are theirs and are rough; the point is the ranking, not the third decimal.

Two structural observations follow, and they are what separates a practitioner who has done this a dozen times from one who has read about it. First, the distribution is extremely skewed: the top three rows account for 39.3 of the 56.5 expected hours, and the bottom four together account for less than one hour. A prompt that states the top five decisions and says nothing about the bottom five captures 93 per cent of the available value at roughly half the writing cost. Second — and this is the observation people miss — the ranking is driven far more by p than by L. The unit question has a loss of 22 hours, but the clock-drift question, with a loss of 14, ranks close behind it because the builder's prior on clock drift is terrible. Loss is something product managers estimate well; p is not, and estimating it is the skill. Low p lives wherever your world differs from the world the builder learned from: house conventions, legacy field names, domain semantics peculiar to your customers, anything decided by a regulator rather than by a convention, and anything that was true when your firmware was written in 2022 and would not be chosen today.

Detection substitutes for specification, but only partly

The harness school's argument can be made in the same notation, which is the fastest way to see both its strength and its limit. Add a detection probability d: the chance that a wrong decision is caught by a test, a type error, a schema validation or a review before it reaches a customer. Then the expected cost of leaving decision i unstated is (1 − pi) · [d · Lcaught + (1 − d) · Lescaped]. Take a decision with p = 0.8, where catching it in review costs 1.5 hours and letting it escape to production costs 22. At d = 0.5 the expected cost is 0.2 × (0.75 + 11) = 2.35 hours. At d = 0.9 it is 0.2 × (1.35 + 2.2) = 0.71 hours. At d = 0.98 it is 0.38 hours. Specifying the decision costs perhaps six minutes, or 0.1 hours. So specification pays off twenty-three times over in a weakly instrumented codebase and still pays off nearly four times over in an exceptionally well-instrumented one — but the gap has narrowed by a factor of six, and at that point the marginal hour is better spent raising d for every decision than raising precision for one.

Figure 3. Specification effort and detection strength are substitutes along a frontier of equal defect escape, but they are not perfect substitutes. Detection cannot catch a decision nobody ever framed as a question — no test exists for a rule nobody wrote — and specification cannot survive contact with a builder whose output nobody checks. Positions far up the vertical axis with nothing on the horizontal are the classic over-specification trap: long, literal prompts producing brittle, unverified code.

The steps practitioners leave implicit

Beyond the familiar translation work — extracting rules from narrative, writing the data contract, stating limits, enumerating edge cases, writing acceptance criteria, declaring non-goals — expert practice contains four moves that rarely appear in any checklist and that both Ira's and Karthik's teams adopted after their incidents.

The first is stating precedence. Real specifications contain constraints that collide: "never block a caller for more than two seconds" and "always confirm identity before disclosing a policy number" are both true and, on a slow backend, incompatible. A human engineer notices the collision and asks. A builder resolves it silently, usually in favour of whichever constraint appeared last or was phrased more emphatically, and the resolution is invisible in the diff. Ira's team now writes a short precedence block at the end of every prompt: which constraint wins, and what the system should do when it cannot satisfy both — in their case, fail closed and hand to a human agent.

The second is bounding the blast radius. The most expensive AI-builder failures in both companies were not wrong features but collateral edits: a shared validation helper "improved" in passing, a configuration default changed to something more sensible in general and wrong for one customer. Expert prompts state what may be changed and, more importantly, what may not: files, modules, public interfaces, database migrations. Shilpan's standing instruction now includes a line that the uplink parser is frozen and any change to it must be proposed as a comment rather than an edit.

The third is choosing vocabulary deliberately, because naming is priming. Asking a builder for a "reconciliation ledger" imports a whole architectural family — append-only records, a settlement cycle, an audit trail — that asking for a "matching table" does not. This is genuinely double-edged: the right domain noun saves paragraphs of specification because it pulls the correct priors in with it, and the wrong one silently imports machinery you will pay to maintain. The tell is generated code that is more elaborate than the problem, containing abstractions nobody asked for; the cause is almost always a noun in the prompt.

The fourth is the counter-example. Adjectives — robust, clean, scalable, graceful — are unfalsifiable and cost nothing to satisfy nominally. A single worked example of a wrong output, labelled as wrong and paired with the correct one, does more to narrow the admissible set than a paragraph of prose, because it disambiguates by demonstration rather than by description. Karthik's rewritten prompt, stripped of everything else, looked like this:

CONTEXT: shilpan-cloud, alerting service. Device payloads come from
firmware v3.x. Do not modify parsers/uplink.py — propose changes as comments.

CONTRACT: reading = { device_id: str, t: ISO-8601 UTC, temp_dc: int
(TENTHS of a degree Celsius, signed), door: 0|1, batt_mv: int }
Thresholds in the product config are in WHOLE degrees Celsius.
Any comparison must convert. temp_dc 42 means 4.2 C, NOT 42 C.

WRONG (produced by the previous generation, do not repeat):
   if reading.temp > config.max_c: raise Excursion()
RIGHT:

PRECEDENCE: if a reading is unparseable, it is a DEVICE FAULT, never an
excursion. Never mark a consignment compliant on the basis of missing data.

Nothing in that block is clever. Every line in it is a decision that had previously lived in Beena's head, in a wiki page, or in a four-year-old commit message.

4. When the practice applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are worth stating as claims that can be checked rather than as advice. Claim one: the correctness of the output is knowable before you look at it. Where you can write down what "right" means in advance, precision in the instruction converts directly into fewer wrong branches. Shilpan satisfies this completely — an excursion either did or did not occur, and the definition is written in a customer's standard operating procedure. Shabdika satisfies it partially: the tool-calling layer has a correct answer per call, but "the agent handled the conversation well" does not, and Ira's team had been treating both halves the same way.

Claim two: the cost of a wrong branch materially exceeds the cost of stating it. This is the inequality from Section 3 and it fails more often than people expect, particularly on internal tools, prototypes and anything with a short half-life. Shilpan passes emphatically: a wrong branch in firmware-adjacent code can take seven months to leave the fleet. Shabdika passes for the tool-calling layer, where a wrong branch touches a regulated disclosure, and fails for the conversational surface, where a clumsy phrasing is corrected in an afternoon.

Claim three: the specification is stable long enough to be worth writing. If the requirement will change before the code ships, precision is inventory, and inventory decays. Karthik's alerting service passes; Ira's agent persona and prompt copy, which the customer's marketing team revised weekly, does not.

Where the idea becomes actively misleading is worth stating with equal force, because the practice has become fashionable enough that it is now applied where it hurts. It misleads on genuinely exploratory work, where precisely specifying an unknown answer merely converts an open question into a confidently wrong implementation that the team will then defend because it is written down. It misleads on aesthetic and experiential judgements, where the vocabulary to state the criterion does not exist until you have seen three candidate outputs — here the dialogic school is straightforwardly correct and the contract-first practitioner will waste a day producing a document that describes nothing anyone wanted. And it misleads, most dangerously, whenever it substitutes for understanding: a precisely specified module that shipped and works, and that nobody on the team can explain at 2 a.m., has traded a visible risk for an invisible one. That is the theory-building objection and it does not go away by being ignored.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

The practice behaves differently, and worse, at boundaries. In a multi-product company the same noun means different things in different products, and a builder given a shared component inherits whichever meaning dominated its training or, worse, whichever meaning appears most often in the repository. Shilpan discovered that "consignment" meant a vehicle load in the telemetry product and a customer order in the billing product, and that a generated reporting module had quietly joined the two. The mature response is not to police prompts but to maintain a small, versioned glossary that every prompt references — and the honest observation is that companies which claim to have one usually have a wiki page nobody has updated in a year.

In two-sided businesses the hardest cases live at the seam rather than on either side. Shrut Bazaar, an Indore-based marketplace for used farm machinery, discovered that neither its buyer-side nor its seller-side specification contained the rule for what happens when a seller relists an item that a buyer has already paid a deposit on — because in each document the other party was a background actor. A builder will not invent that rule; it will not even notice the gap, because each half of the specification is internally coherent. The practitioner's move is to specify seams as first-class objects: for every transaction, write the state machine both parties share, and prompt from the state machine rather than from either party's story.

In regulated contexts the specification acquires an author outside the company, and this changes the character of the work rather than its volume. A builder's prior on what is reasonable is drawn from a world where the reasonable thing is usually permitted; regulators exist precisely where that is untrue. Both the IRDAI disclosure norms in Ira's case and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's consent and retention requirements in Shabdika's call-recording pipeline create rules that are arbitrary from the builder's point of view and non-negotiable from the company's. The expert practice is to quote the obligation in the prompt rather than paraphrasing it, and to write the acceptance criterion as the auditor would test it, not as the engineer would.

In hardware-plus-software the asymmetry of reversibility dominates everything. Shilpan's cloud code can be redeployed in eleven minutes; its firmware reaches the whole fleet in seven months. That asymmetry means the two halves of a contract must be specified to completely different standards of rigour, and it means the interface between them should be treated as frozen and quoted verbatim into every prompt rather than described. The failure Karthik hit was not a firmware bug and not a cloud bug; it was an interface whose semantics existed only in the head of the person who wrote one side.

In AI-native products, where the thing being built is itself non-deterministic, the acceptance criterion changes species. Ira could not write "the agent shall ask the caller to disambiguate when multiple policies match" as a pass/fail test in the way Karthik could write a threshold comparison, because the agent's behaviour is statistical. What she could write is an evaluation: a labelled set of 340 multi-policy conversations, a required disambiguation rate above 99 per cent, and a hard rule implemented outside the model — the tool layer refuses to return a policy number when the lookup is ambiguous. The general principle, and it is the most important sentence in this section, is that when the builder is non-deterministic and the artefact is non-deterministic, precision migrates out of the prose and into the evaluation set and the deterministic guardrails around the model. Teams that keep trying to specify their way to reliability in prose, when the artefact itself is probabilistic, are solving the previous decade's problem.

At the organisational seams, what mature companies actually do diverges from what they describe. The stated process is that the product manager writes the specification, an engineer writes the prompt, the output is reviewed and merged. The observed process, in both these companies and in most others, is that prompts accumulate in individual engineers' chat histories, are never versioned with the code, are re-invented weekly, and drift from the specification they were derived from within about two sprints. The companies that handle this well do one unglamorous thing: they keep the prompt in the repository next to the code it generated, review it as part of the diff, and treat a change to the prompt as a change to the system. That is a filing decision, not a technical one, and it is the single highest-return organisational intervention in this whole topic.
