6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The expensive ambiguity is usually a noun, not a verb. Competent practitioners polish verbs — should, must, will — and leave the nouns undefined. But a noun like "active customer", "settled batch" or "consignment" carries an entire rule set: a time window, an inclusion test, a tie-break. The tell in the wild is two people in the same meeting quoting different numbers for the same metric and neither noticing; that disagreement is a specification defect that has been sitting in the codebase for months. The obvious reading — that the verbs carry the requirements — is wrong because verbs describe what happens while nouns define what it happens to, and a builder cannot get the former right if the latter is undetermined.

Silence is an instruction, and it always resolves to the corpus mode. Omitting a rule does not leave a hole; it delegates the decision to whatever pattern is most common in the builder's training, which is a generic SaaS application built by people who have never seen your customers. The tell is generated code that is idiomatic for a company you do not work at: standard field names where yours are legacy, a retry policy calibrated for a web API where yours talks to a cellular modem. The obvious reading is that unstated things are neutral; they are not neutral, they are opinionated in a direction you did not choose.

Precision has a right-hand side. Beyond some point, more constraint produces literal compliance: the builder does exactly what was said and stops thinking, discarding priors that would have served you well. The tell is a diff that satisfies every stated requirement and that the reviewing engineer describes as "technically correct and somehow awful" — no error handling beyond the cases you listed, no reuse of an obvious existing helper, a structure that mirrors the sequence of your bullet points rather than the shape of the problem. The obvious reading, that a longer prompt is a safer prompt, is wrong because a prompt is not only a constraint on output but a signal about how much latitude the builder has.

Fluency is uncorrelated with correctness on your domain. Generated code arrives well-formatted, well-commented and confident, and human reviewers calibrate trust on exactly those surface signals because that is what they have always been able to calibrate on. The tell is a comment that confidently explains a business rule nobody ever stated — "we take the most recently updated policy here since that is the one the caller is most likely asking about" — which is the builder narrating its own guess in the register of institutional knowledge. Ira's incident was hiding behind precisely such a comment for eleven days. The obvious reading, that well-documented code is well-understood code, inverts the causality: the documentation was generated from the same guess as the code.

State the precedence, not just the constraints. Competent practitioners list constraints; experts list what wins when two collide, and what the system should do when it can satisfy neither. The tell is a system that behaves correctly in every individual test and wrongly under load, because the collision only materialises when the backend is slow. The obvious reading is that constraints are independent; in real systems they are jointly satisfiable only in the normal case, and the abnormal case is the whole reason the code exists.

Specify the blast radius before the behaviour. Most reviewers read a diff for whether it does the right thing; few read it for whether it touched things it had no business touching. The tell is a pull request whose file list is longer than the feature justifies — a shared utility "tidied up", a default changed, a dependency upgraded. Experts write the boundary into the prompt before the requirement, because a correct feature that broke an unrelated module is a net loss and, unlike a wrong feature, it usually ships. The obvious reading — that improvements are improvements — ignores that an unrequested change has no test written for it and no one watching it.

Nouns prime architecture. Vocabulary choice imports design, and the import is silent. Ask for a "workflow engine" and you will get one, with states, transitions and a persistence layer, whether or not the problem needed more than an if-statement. The tell is generated code that is one abstraction level more elaborate than the problem: interfaces with a single implementation, configuration for a thing that will never vary. The obvious reading is that vocabulary is presentation; in fact vocabulary is the highest-leverage compression available in a prompt, and like all compression it can decompress into something you did not intend.

One good generation is a sample, not an outcome. This is the point most competent practitioners can recite and few act on. The tell is a team that cannot answer the question "if you ran that prompt again tomorrow, how different would the result be?" — not because the answer is bad but because nobody has ever checked. Experts re-run deliberately on anything consequential and read the diff between generations, because the places where two runs disagree are exactly the places where the instruction was under-determined, and that diff is the cheapest ambiguity detector in existence. The obvious reading — that a working result validates the prompt — confuses the sample with the distribution.

The prompt must be re-runnable, which makes it code. A prompt that cannot be found, cannot be re-run; a module that cannot be regenerated has to be maintained by hand, which was supposedly the thing being avoided. The tell is a team six weeks on that cannot reproduce how a module came to exist and has started patching it manually. Experts version the prompt with the code and update it when the code changes, accepting that this is a real maintenance cost. The obvious reading — that the prompt is scaffolding you discard once the code stands up — is wrong for the same reason a build script is not scaffolding.

Review capacity, not prompt quality, is the binding constraint. This is the hardest one for an enthusiastic team to accept, and it is the one Naur's argument predicts. A team can improve its prompts indefinitely and still be limited by how much generated code its engineers can genuinely understand per week — not skim, understand well enough to modify under pressure. The tell is a team whose throughput rose and whose incident mean-time-to-repair also rose; another is an on-call engineer who, looking at a module, has to read it from scratch to answer a question. The obvious reading, that better instructions reduce the need for comprehension, gets the relationship backwards: better instructions increase how much code arrives per unit time, and therefore increase the comprehension debt unless review depth rises with it.

7. What actually differs across product types and stages

Much of the advice in circulation about prompting varies by product type more than it should. The translation mechanics — contract, limits, edge cases, precedence, non-goals, blast radius — do not change at all between a consumer app and an enterprise platform. What changes is where the low-p decisions cluster, which is to say where your world diverges most from the builder's prior, and what an acceptance criterion can even look like.

The advice that is genuinely stage-independent is short: write the units down, and write down what must not change.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Shabdika: from prose precision to statistical acceptance

Ira's team did not fix the disambiguation bug by writing a better sentence, although they wrote one. They did three things and measured each. They added a hard guardrail in the tool layer: a policy lookup returning more than one match raises a specific ambiguity signal that the model cannot override, which converted a probabilistic behaviour into a deterministic one and removed the decision from the builder's hands entirely. They built a labelled evaluation set of 340 conversations drawn from real multi-policy calls, and made "disambiguation rate ≥ 99.0 per cent" an acceptance criterion in the prompt itself, so that the builder was told how its output would be judged. And they rewrote the eleven-word sentence into a nine-line contract. The incidence of the wrong-policy disclosure fell from roughly 1 in 300 calls on the affected customer's traffic to zero over the following 62,000 calls. Of the three interventions, the team's own judgement — reached by disabling each in a staging replay — was that the guardrail accounted for most of the improvement, the evaluation set for most of the confidence, and the rewritten sentence for the smallest share. That ordering is uncomfortable for a page about prompting and is the honest result.

Shilpan: the unit that cost two days and eleven crore of stock reports

Karthik's numbers are cleaner. The unit error flagged 217 consignments across four distributors as excursions over two days. Nothing was written off, because the distributors' own staff disbelieved the alerts — which is its own lesson about a system that cries wolf — but Shilpan's team spent 22 engineer-hours on detection and correction, and the customer-facing consequence was a formal quality query from the largest distributor that took Karthik personally three weeks to close. Against that, the line in the prompt that would have prevented it took four minutes to write and is fourteen words long. The team's post-incident change was not just that line but a standing header, now attached to every prompt against the alerting service, containing the frozen uplink contract with units, the glossary of seven domain nouns, and the blast-radius restriction. In the four features generated after that change, the count of decisions left open fell from nineteen to six, expected wrong decisions from 2.85 to 0.7, and measured rework from an average of 21 hours per feature to 4.

Shrut Bazaar: where more precision made things worse

The failure is more instructive than either success. Shrut Bazaar's head of product, Vikram Deshpande, had read the same arguments and applied them enthusiastically to a listing-quality score — a model-assisted rating meant to push well-photographed, honestly described tractors and harvesters up the search results. He wrote a fourteen-page prompt: 31 numbered rules, weightings to two decimal places, a rubric for photograph quality, penalties for missing fields. The builder complied exactly. The score shipped in April 2026 and within nine days the marketplace's supply side had visibly contracted: listings from smaller dealers, who photographed equipment on a phone in a yard rather than in a shed with lighting, had been systematically pushed below the fold. Gross merchandise value on the affected categories fell about 12 per cent over three weeks. Two of the 31 rules interacted in a way nobody had modelled, and because the weights were specified to two decimals, nobody could tell which two.

The diagnosis was not imprecision; it was precision applied to a problem whose answer nobody knew. Vikram had specified a rubric when what he possessed was an intuition, and the specification had laundered the intuition into something that looked authoritative and could not be questioned. The recovery took five weeks and inverted the approach entirely. The team deleted the rubric, assembled 600 listings hand-ranked by two experienced category managers, and rewrote the prompt to about a page: build a scorer, here is the labelled set, here is the agreement threshold, here is the constraint that no single photographic feature may move a listing more than one decile. Precision migrated from the prose to the data, which is exactly the harness school's prescription, and the score that eventually shipped in June agreed with the human rankings 84 per cent of the time against the rubric version's 61. The lesson Vikram states, when asked, is deliberately awkward: the fourteen-page prompt was not a failure of prompting technique. It was a correct technique applied to a problem that did not have a specification yet, and the technique's very competence is what made the error expensive to see.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Four disagreements are live, and none of them is settled by the evidence currently available. Each is stated below in the strongest form its adherents would recognise, with what would have to be true for it to be wrong.

Specify first, or discover by iterating. The contract-first position, at full strength: the decisions in a specification exist whether or not you write them down, and iterating with a builder does not remove them, it merely conceals which ones were made and by whom. A team that iterates to a working result has a system whose rules live nowhere, cannot be audited, and cannot be re-derived when a regulator or a customer asks why. Its evidence is the defect-cost gradient — a rule settled before generation costs minutes, the same rule settled after release costs days — and the observation that the modules people cannot explain are disproportionately the ones that were converged on rather than specified. The dialogic position, at full strength: specification effort ahead of feedback is speculative inventory, most of which is waste, because you cannot know in advance which unstated decisions the builder will get wrong, and a single generation tells you more about that than an hour of imagining. Its evidence is throughput: teams that generate early consistently reach a working candidate faster, and the candidate itself functions as the cheapest possible specification review. The contract-first position would be wrong if the decisions that matter were reliably visible in the first generation's output — and on well-trodden problems they mostly are. The dialogic position would be wrong if the expensive defects were systematically the invisible ones, the ones a generation looks fine on — and in regulated and hardware contexts they systematically are. Both camps are generalising correctly from different populations of problem.

Prose, or executable ground truth. The harness position: prose is a channel with no verification, and every hour spent improving it competes with an hour spent on a fixture, a type or a failing test that constrains the builder mechanically and keeps constraining it next month. Its evidence is variance — re-run a prose-only prompt and outputs diverge; re-run one anchored to tests and they converge. The writing-craft position: tests specify what you already know to check, and the whole difficulty is the decisions you have not yet thought to test; prose is the only medium in which you can state an intention you cannot yet operationalise, and it is the medium in which a human colleague can spot that your intention is wrong. The harness position would be wrong if most defects were in decisions nobody had framed as a question — and Shrut's failure is exactly that case. The writing position would be wrong if prose precision showed a low ceiling in practice, which Shabdika's own disabling experiment suggests it might.

Who should write the prompt. One camp holds that the product manager should drive the builder directly, because every hand-off loses intent and the person who knows what "settled" means should be the one saying it. The other holds that the prompt is an engineering artefact — it references file paths, interfaces and invariants — and that a product manager writing it produces either vagueness or, worse, confident architectural instruction she is not placed to give. The first camp's evidence is cycle time and fidelity at small companies. The second's is the observation that PM-written prompts skew toward over-specifying implementation, which is the very failure mode with the most expensive tail. This disagreement is not resolvable in general and both camps quietly converge on the same practice at scale: the PM owns the contract and the acceptance criteria, the engineer owns the context, the boundary and the harness, and they are written in one document that both sign.

Whether non-determinism is a defect to eliminate or variance to exploit. The engineering instinct is to drive variance to zero: pin the model, fix the temperature, make generation reproducible, treat two different outputs from one prompt as a bug in the prompt. The opposing view, held by a smaller but serious group, is that variance is free search — generate five candidates, have the harness reject four, and you have used the builder's uncertainty rather than fighting it, at a cost that is now trivial. Its evidence is that on well-tested code paths, best-of-n materially beats best-effort-single. Its weakness is that it only works where the acceptance criterion is mechanical, and it can hide under-specification behind a selection step: if you are picking the run that looks right, you are supplying the missing specification with your eyes and not writing it down. The first view would be wrong if detection were near-perfect; the second would be wrong if the criteria you select against were themselves incomplete — which is the normal case.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes longer prompts. Someone who has internalised it writes differently shaped ones and, on many days, shorter ones. The visible behaviours are surprisingly consistent across the practitioners worth learning from. They spend the first few minutes on a feature not writing but listing the decisions the instruction leaves open, and they rank that list by where the builder's prior is likely to be worst rather than by what matters most to the business — because those two orderings are different, and confusing them is the commonest error among smart, experienced people. They reach for a counter-example before an adjective. They can tell you, for any module their team shipped last quarter, what the prompt said and where it lives. They treat a review finding as a defect in the instruction rather than in the output, and they update the instruction, which is the habit that compounds.

Less visibly, they hold the schools of thought lightly and situationally. On a firmware interface they are contract-first without apology; on a new interaction pattern nobody has seen, they are dialogic and will refuse to write a rubric; on anything shipping into a regulated disclosure they invest in guardrails outside the model rather than in more emphatic prose. Asked which approach is correct, they answer with a question about reversibility and about how correctness will be known. And they retain, under pressure, the willingness to say that the team does not yet know what right looks like — which is the single most valuable sentence in this whole discipline, because it is the one that stops a precisely specified wrong answer from being built beautifully and defended for a quarter.

12. What each of them decided

Ira's decision, taken on 29 May, was to stop treating precision as a property of prose in a probabilistic system. Shabdika now classifies every behaviour in the agent as either a hard rule, implemented deterministically in the tool layer and specified as a contract with a test, or a model judgement, specified as an evaluation set with a threshold and no prose criterion at all. The classification itself is a product decision she owns, and the rule she applies is regulatory and financial exposure: anything an auditor or a regulator could ask her to demonstrate becomes a hard rule, whatever it costs in conversational naturalness. The tool-calling prompt shrank from three pages to one. The evaluation set grew from nothing to 1,900 labelled conversations.

Karthik's decision, taken the same week, was narrower and more institutional. Shilpan now maintains a single frozen-interface header — units, field semantics, glossary, blast radius — that is included verbatim at the top of every prompt touching the telemetry pipeline, is versioned in the repository beside the parser it describes, and is updated only through the same review that governs a firmware change. He did not adopt a prompting methodology, hire a specialist or buy a tool. He wrote down, once, the things that had only ever existed in the head of the engineer who built the device, and he made re-reading them the price of generating anything. On his own accounting, that header is worth more than every other change his team made in the quarter, and it took an afternoon.

Three questions for discussion. First: Shabdika's own experiment suggested the rewritten prompt contributed least to the fix, behind the guardrail and the evaluation set — under what circumstances should a team conclude that its prompting problem is really an architecture problem, and what would the evidence look like? Second: Vikram at Shrut Bazaar applied a technique correctly to a problem that was not ready for it, and the technique's competence made the error harder to see — what test would have distinguished, on the day he started writing, between a problem with a knowable specification and one that needed labelled data instead? Third: Table 3 shows the specification phase unchanged at six hours across all three regimes while everything else collapsed — if the essential difficulty is genuinely untouched by these tools, what should a product organisation actually do with the capacity the tools released, and what is the argument against simply building more?

13. Going deeper

AI-assisted building sits underneath everything here: what the tools can and cannot do, where they are reliable and where they are confidently wrong, is the substrate on which any prompting judgement rests, and without it a practitioner is calibrating p by folklore. The spec as a prompt for an AI builder is the natural next move — designing the specification document so its structure already carries the contract, limits, precedence and non-goals, which collapses two artefacts into one and removes the translation seam where most intent is lost. Reviewing work you did not write is the constraint this whole page keeps running into: the value of precise instruction evaporates entirely if nobody can tell whether the output honoured it, and the theory-building objection is only answerable through review practice.

Four topics supply the technical vocabulary that makes a prompt precise rather than merely long. How web and mobile apps work tells you which behaviours belong to the client, the server or the network, and therefore which constraints are even addressable in the module being built. APIs and integration basics is where contracts, versioning and backward compatibility live, and a practitioner who cannot read an interface definition cannot specify one. Data modelling for PMs is the discipline behind the observation that the expensive ambiguity is a noun: entities, keys, cardinality and the difference between one policy and the set of a customer's policies, which is precisely what cost Shabdika eleven days. Databases, storage and caching explains why some constraints are cheap and others are not, and stops a specification from demanding something the storage layer cannot give.

Finally, cloud infrastructure basics and reading an architecture diagram determine how far the blast radius of a generated change can reach and whether you can see it. A practitioner who can read the architecture can state what a prompt must not touch; one who cannot is writing boundaries in the dark and will find them, eventually, by breaking one.

Shabdika Speech Cloud, Shilpan Instruments and Shrut Bazaar are illustrative composites created for teaching purposes; the individuals named are fictional. The Reserve Bank of India, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act appear as market context only. All figures are constructed to demonstrate the mechanics under discussion and should not be read as benchmarks.
